children: It's been an eventful month on bond markets to say the least, with Treasury yields soaring to levels not seen since the early days of the financial crisis almost two decades ago.

I'm sure you know all about that by now. But there's something else that's caught my attention today: The premium that investors demand for holding longer-dated government bonds over shorter-dated ones is narrowing, making the so-called yield curve flatter.
A full inversion, when two-year yields exceed 10-year yields, has often presaged a recession in the past.
It suggests investors believe the Fed is going to raise short-term interest rates to the extent that the economy slows or contracts.

On average, the lead time to a recession has been 15 months, analysts at Evercore ISI said in a note yesterday. The longest lag was almost three years after the curve inverted, in 1978. The shortest, five months, followed the 2019 inversion. We'll never know, but the curve might have gotten lucky that time, since it was the pandemic-unknowable before it struck-that caused the subsequent recession.

The stock market peaks then starts to tumble nine months, on average, after the yield curve inverts, the Evercore analysts say. They think the current bull market is safe for now, not least because the curve hasn't yet inverted.
